messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 75
- Gender: Non-binary
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Financial Analyst
- Trauma Type: Rape
- Pcl5: 58

At 75, they still keep spreadsheets for everything. Grocery costs, dividend dates, medication refills, the birthdays of grandchildren and great-nieces spread across two countries. Numbers have been their way of steadying the world for decades, first in a bank and later as a financial analyst consulting part-time after formal retirement. They say that numbers “behave better than people.” It sounds like a joke when they first offer it, but over time it becomes clear that it is also a summary of how they have survived.

The assault happened many years ago, after their spouse was already gone. They had been widowed for three years and were still learning the strange choreography of being alone. One evening, after staying late to finish reports at a client office, they accepted a ride from a man they knew professionally, someone they had spoken with many times and had no reason to fear. They remember the ordinary details with painful clarity: the glow of dashboard lights, the smell of stale coffee in the car, rain beginning on the windshield. What happened next lives in their mind not as a single memory but as fragments that break through without warning. The sudden shift in his voice. Their own disbelief. Their body going rigid while their thoughts became strangely distant, as if they were watching from above and calculating impossible odds. Later they would say, in the flat tone they use for market losses, that they “stopped being a person for a while and became an object.”

In the days after, they do what they have always done in crisis: they organize. They cancel meetings, draft practical emails, wash their clothes twice, then again, as if precision might erase what has happened. They do not tell family. They do not go to the police. They are ashamed of having accepted the ride, ashamed of their age, ashamed that a person who has negotiated contracts and managed portfolios could have been overpowered so completely. At night they lie awake, exhausted but unable to sleep. Each time they begin to drift off, they jerk back into alertness with their heart pounding, seeing his hand on the steering wheel, hearing the click of the door lock. Mornings become a performance of normality: pressed shirt, tidy kitchen, market news on the radio, all while nausea sits just under the surface.

They return to work quickly, telling themselves that routine is stabilizing. In some ways, it is. At a desk, with columns to reconcile and forecasts to revise, their mind narrows to something measurable. But the office also becomes full of threat. They startle when men approach from behind. If someone lowers their voice or stands too close at the copier, their skin prickles and their thoughts scatter. They begin taking the stairs to avoid enclosed elevators. They position themselves nearest to exits in conference rooms and restaurants. Colleagues notice that they no longer stay late, no longer attend networking dinners, no longer tolerate even casual physical contact. They explain it away as aging, fatigue, grief.

The worst times are the moments that should be quiet. A rainy evening. Keys in a car ignition. The scent of aftershave on a stranger at the supermarket. Then the past surges forward with such force that the present disappears. Their chest tightens, their hands go cold, and they feel again the same helpless certainty that they are trapped. Sometimes they lose pieces of time, standing in the kitchen with no memory of why they walked there. Sometimes they wake from dreams soaked in sweat, not always seeing the assault itself but sensing pursuit, pressure, a terrible inability to speak. They keep lights on through the night and check the locks multiple times, then feel foolish and angry with themselves for doing it.

Over the years, they become smaller in their life. They decline invitations, especially in the evening. They stop traveling alone. They screen every phone call. Intimacy of any kind becomes fraught. After being widowed they had once imagined companionship might still be possible in late life, but now even a warm, interested conversation can trigger suspicion and a wish to flee. They feel cut off from their own body, as if it is unreliable terrain. Some days they look in the mirror and feel tenderness for the older person staring back; other days they feel only contempt, hearing an inner voice that says they should have known better, fought harder, spoken sooner.

What troubles them most in the present is not only fear, but the persistence of it. They resent that a single act of violence continues to shape daily choices so many years later. When they review a client’s retirement projections, they can still think clearly and spot patterns others miss. Yet outside that familiar competence, they remain vigilant, scanning parking lots, memorizing exits, gauging every man’s distance and tone. They often feel detached during family gatherings, smiling at the right moments while part of them stays on watch. They speak of grief for their spouse and grief for the self they were before the assault as if these are braided together now. “I keep functioning,” they say. “That’s not the same as feeling safe.”
